# Structural Honesty Dissertation — Canonical Audit Ledger

**Pre-Publication Working Draft — Working iteration as of May 12, 2026**

This is the source-of-truth claim-tracking ledger for the dissertation. It maps each major claim in Chapter 1 and the outline to its backing source (existing citation in the bibliography) or its future proof obligation (specific chapter where the claim is rigorously developed). The ledger is itself an instance of Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency) applied to the dissertation's own claim-tracking substrate: every claim made on the working surface pre-v1.0, and on the public surface from v1.0 onward, should map to either a present argument, a cited source, an explicit future proof obligation, a named open problem, a scope exclusion, or a continuation commitment.

**Authorship and contribution accounting** (per cycle-27 AI-Collaboration Attribution Statement and Discipline disclosure, cycle-27R+P propagation): Bilal Syed Arfeen (BayyinahEnterprise) is primary author with final dispositive authority. Claude Opus 4.7 via claude.ai web interface (Anthropic, May 2026) is lead analytical synthesizer responsible for ledger entry drafting under project-lead direction. Audit team contributions across cycles 1-27R per AI-Collaboration Attribution Statement §1.1 enumeration. Operational-substrate-capacity constraint disclosed at cycle-27R per Pattern I (forward-tracked).

Future audits extend this markdown directly. The companion HTML presentation surface (`audit-ledger-perplexity-v1.html`, authored by Perplexity) is an archived presentation snapshot; future HTML views may be regenerated from this markdown ledger at checkpoints (end-of-May after Chapters 2–3, end-of-July after Part IV, at v1.0 publication), with each generated view separately versioned. The canonical source-of-truth ledger remains this markdown document.

## Status legend

- **drafted** — Claim is stated in the current pre-publication draft with present argument
- **cited** — Claim is supported by an existing citation in the bibliography
- **proof-obligation** — Claim is forwarded to a specific chapter for rigorous development
- **proven** — Claim has been rigorously demonstrated in the assigned chapter and survived the relevant audit pass
- **independently verified** — A cited claim has been corroborated by an external source or replication independent of the original program source
- **named-open** — Claim is named as an open problem with no v1.0 proof commitment
- **continuation** — Claim is part of the post-v1.0 multi-decade roadmap
- **scope-exclusion** — Claim is explicitly excluded from v1.0 scope
- **superseded** — Claim remains in the historical ledger but is no longer active; successor row is linked (post-v1.0 only)
- **withdrawn** — Claim is explicitly withdrawn; reason and successor state recorded (post-v1.0 only)

The outline's Preservation discipline section operationalizes these into six implementation mechanisms. The two lists are not identical; they overlap but the granularity and naming differ. ## Section 10: Chapter 2 ledger rows (specification-first, pre-prose)

These rows are drafted before Chapter 2 prose is written, per the specification-first discipline. Each row identifies a claim that Chapter 2 will need to make, the source that backs it, and (where relevant) the future chapter that discharges any forwarded proof obligation. Chapter 2 prose will then be written against these rows rather than retrofitted afterward.

Chapter 2's title is "Historical and Intellectual Context." It identifies three convergent intellectual lineages that have independently approached the structural-honesty problem and argues that the dissertation's contribution is their synthesis under a unified axiomatic framework.

### Sub-outline: Chapter 2 §§3-4 (audit-and-assurance and textual-preservation philology lineages)

| H4.1 | §3.1 — Double-entry bookkeeping (Pacioli 1494) and the origin of reconciliation discipline. Pacioli's *Tractatus XI* (within the *Summa* [pacioli1494]) is the canonical early printed codification of double-entry bookkeeping as a systematic reconciliation discipline: each transaction recorded as both a debit and a credit, with the two records constrained to reconcile arithmetically. Earlier accounting, administrative-archive, legal-record, and scribal-control practices may have anticipated reconciliation-like disciplines; the dissertation's claim is restricted to Pacioli's role as the canonical early printed codification, not to global historical priority | H4 + H5 (exemplar of reconciliation discipline) | cited + proof-obligation |
| H4.2 | §3.2 — From bookkeeping to professional audit to modern financial-reporting regimes. The five-century evolution from Pacioli through Renaissance/early-modern commercial practice to professional audit to modern GAAP/IFRS-style reporting [previts1979history]. Modern regimes use multiple required or customary projections — such as statements of financial position, performance, cash flows, equity changes, and explanatory notes — constrained to be mutually consistent under defined accounting identities. The specific projection set is modern and jurisdiction-dependent; the substantive claim is that multi-projection-consistency discipline is the structural pattern, not that any specific projection list is universal | H4 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H4.3 | §3.3 — Security-audit frameworks as multi-control projection regimes. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 [iso27001], NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 [nist80053], and SOC 2-style attestation regimes underwritten by the AICPA Trust Services Criteria [aicpa2017tsc] share a multi-control-projection-with-attestation pattern: an organization declares scope, the controls within scope, implementation evidence per control, and audit trail of each control's operation; mutual consistency across these declarations is the audit's empirical content | H4 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H4.4 | §3.4 — Supply-chain audit as the four-substrate stack. The sigstore/in-toto/SLSA lineage provides identity, process, and institutional-maturity substrates respectively, and composes with SHV's semantic substrate to form the four-substrate stack [arfeen2026shvsupplychain]. §3.4 establishes the historical lineage only; the four-substrate composition itself is treated in Chapter 16 | H4 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H4.5 | §3.5 — What the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes to AX-SH. The lineage contributes the practical reconciliation discipline behind Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency) and the operational severity vocabulary (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW). Double-entry bookkeeping is the historical exemplar of reconciliation discipline rather than a full formal precursor. The lineage does not contribute Axioms 1, 2, or 3 (treated in §2) | H5 | proof-obligation |

#### §4: Textual-preservation philology lineage (5 subsections, ~3-4 pages, boundary discipline preserved)

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| H6.1 | §4.1 — Vedic oral transmission and Sanskrit philological traditions. Vedic oral transmission, practiced over millennia, used multiple memorization patterns (samhitā-pāṭha, pada-pāṭha, krama-pāṭha, jaṭā-pāṭha, ghana-pāṭha) to provide redundancy against transmission error. Pāṇini's *Aṣṭādhyāyī* provided a formal grammatical anchor that constrained linguistic forms with rule-based precision. Staal's 1986 analysis [staal1986fidelity] treats Vedic transmission as a verification substrate operating with high redundancy across independent transmitters. Vedic transmission and Pāṇinian grammar are distinct traditions; the section preserves that distinction per the H6 correction | H6 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H6.2 | §4.2 — Quranic preservation as multi-substrate verification (with boundary discipline). The Quranic preservation tradition combines independent verification substrates including hifz (memorization across large communities of reciters), manuscript transmission with documented orthographic discipline, recitation protocol (tajwid, with mutawatir chains of transmission), the riwayat tradition of variant transmissions, and mass communal verification through congregational practice [farrin2010surat, arfeen2026shv]. The formalization of mass-transmission redundancy (the *n*-witness or tawatur-style analysis) is deferred to Chapter 11 where the formal information-theoretic-style redundancy framework is developed; §4.2 describes the operational practice without committing to a specific numerical formalism. The structural-honesty framework treats this as one of the strongest historical instances of multi-substrate textual preservation per QR1; the framework does not adjudicate the tradition's theological content, religious truth claims, or scriptural status. This boundary is the §4 equivalent of the §1 "no retroactive attribution" discipline | H6 + QR1 boundary | cited + proof-obligation |
| H6.3 | §4.3 — Talmudic and Masoretic textual-criticism traditions. The Masoretic tradition (roughly 7th-10th centuries CE) developed systematic textual-criticism practices for the Hebrew Bible, including consonantal/vocalized text distinction, marginal note systems (Masorah parva, Masorah magna), and qere/ketib variant cataloging, anchored in Tov's textual-criticism work [tov2012textual]. The Talmudic tradition developed attributional and dialectical practices that preserve named authorities, variant readings, and argumentative contexts, providing a multi-witness substrate for textual and interpretive transmission, anchored in Strack-Stemberger [strack1996introduction]. These traditions exemplify preserving variants alongside the preferred text, with cross-witness comparison as the empirical basis for textual decisions. Same boundary discipline as §4.2: verification-substrate description, not religious adjudication | H6 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H6.4 | §4.4 — Classical philology and Lachmann's stemmatic method. The classical philological tradition culminated in Karl Lachmann's 19th-century stemmatic method, which formalized reconstructing an archetype text from derivative manuscripts by tracing genealogical relationships through shared errors [timpanaro2005lachmann]. Each surviving manuscript is treated as a projection of the archetype; cross-manuscript collation provides the empirical basis for archetype reconstruction. Reynolds-Wilson [reynolds2013scribes] treats this lineage comprehensively | H6 | cited + proof-obligation |
| H6.5 | §4.5 — What the textual-preservation philology lineage contributes to AX-SH. The lineage contributes the centuries-scale preservation discipline (the seven durability principles of Chapter 1 §4) and the multi-substrate redundancy intuition. This is the lineage that grounds the framework's centuries-scale durability claim. The lineage does not supply the dissertation's primary mathematical anchors for Axioms 1-3 (those are formal-verification contributions, §2); philological and grammatical traditions including Pāṇinian formalism do contribute mathematical structure of their own, but not the specific formal-methods structure used for Axioms 1-3 in this dissertation. The lineage's principal contribution is the operational preservation discipline that the framework adopts. The boundary between verification-substrate description and religious-content adjudication is preserved throughout | H7 + QR1 boundary | proof-obligation |

No claim outside H4-H7 + QR1 boundary is introduced; if the prose later introduces a claim not covered by these sub-rows, that itself signals drift and should trigger either a sub-row addition or a prose correction.

**Sub-outline audit risks (for the spec-only audit pass before prose drafting).** Four specific risks identified by ChatGPT in the §§5-7 sub-outline review, recorded here as auditable discipline:

1. **Synthesis overclaim.** §5 must not claim that AX-SH solves what the three lineages missed; it must claim AX-SH proposes a synthesis whose formal adequacy is deferred to Theorem 8.3. H8.5 enforces this discipline at the ledger level.
2. **Exemplar inflation.** §6 must never treat a historical exemplar as equivalent to the final axiom. The safe pattern is "historical exemplar / motivating structure / primary anchor," not "this tradition already contained Axiom X." H9.5 enforces this at the ledger level.
3. **Lineage caricature.** §7 must not unfairly flatten the traditions. Formal verification has preservation-relevant work (proof archives, mechanized theorem-library maintenance); audit has mathematical structure (the accounting-identity arithmetic at the foundation of GAAP/IFRS); philology has formal structures (Pāṇinian grammar, stemmatic-reconstruction algorithms). Each lineage's gap is specific: it did not develop the particular structural piece that AX-SH requires, in the form AX-SH requires it. The body text of H10.1-H10.3 enforces this discipline by describing what each lineage *did* develop before noting the specific gap.
4. **Recursive scope discipline.** §7's "what each lineage did not develop" framing must be explicitly relative to AX-SH, not as a universal critique. The lineages are not failing at things they did not attempt; they are simply not the locations where the specific synthesis AX-SH proposes was developed. The phrase "did not develop X" rather than "missed X" is the operational implementation of this discipline at the row-title level.

Identify (a) any claim not covered by H8-H10 or its sub-rows, (b) any exemplar inflated into an axiom-equivalence claim (the H9.5 discipline), (c) any unfair caricature of a lineage (the H10 discipline of describing what each lineage did develop before noting the specific gap), (d) any place where §7 understates what a lineage actually did develop in order to make AX-SH appear more novel (the complementary risk to caricature: not flattening the lineage's strengths to inflate the synthesis claim), (e) any synthesis claim that outruns Chapter 8's Theorem 8.3 proof obligation (the H8.5 discipline), and (f) any place where the prose retroactively attributes SHV terminology or SHV-equivalent intent to historical figures or traditions (the H8.3 discipline / the §1 boundary). Do not review style except where wording creates a structural-honesty risk."

**Prose-discipline notes for §§5-7 (carried forward from the spec-only audit pass).** Four notes describe specific prose-level disciplines that should travel forward into the §§5-7 drafting phase. They are not ledger defects; they are guidance for how the audited sub-outline should be discharged into prose:

1. **H8.4 interpretive framing.** The "three lineages as partial projections of a broader verification problem" framing is the dissertation's interpretive reading, not an objective historical claim. The §5.4 prose should make this status explicit, e.g., "From the dissertation's perspective, the three lineages can be read as partial projections..." rather than asserting the projection structure as a historical fact about the lineages themselves.
2. **H10.1 prose discipline.** Before stating the formal-verification gap, §7.1 prose should acknowledge that formal verification does maintain proof artifacts, theorem libraries, and mechanized verification infrastructures; the narrower point is that it did not develop the dissertation's seven-part centuries-scale preservation discipline as part of its core verification theory.
3. **H10.2 prose discipline.** Before stating the audit gap, §7.2 prose should acknowledge accounting identities, sampling theory, risk-assessment models, and standards-logic apparatus; the narrower point is that audit did not develop a unified AX-SH-style axiom system spanning all its substrates.
4. **H10.3 prose discipline.** Before stating the philology gap, §7.3 prose should acknowledge computational stemmatics, Pāṇinian formal grammar, and philological method (collation algorithms, conjectural emendation rules); the narrower point is that the lineage did not develop the specific automated static verification or substrate-extraction machinery that AX-SH requires.

These four notes operationalize the lineage-caricature and lineage-understatement risks identified by the §§5-7 spec-only audit. The post-prose audit prompt's clauses (c) and (d) are the matched detectors for whether the prose actually executes these disciplines.

## Section 11: Chapter 3 ledger rows (mathematical prerequisites, specification-first, pre-prose)

Chapter 3 introduces the mathematical apparatus that Chapters 4-8 use to formalize Axioms 1-4. Where Chapter 2 supplied the historical and intellectual context, Chapter 3 supplies the formal prerequisites: the categorical, relation-theoretic, type-theoretic, and projection-consistency machinery that the four axioms are expressed against. The parent MP-rows below are canon for the parent-level specification following one focused spec-only dual-audit pass (both auditors converged on PASS, with ChatGPT recommending six wording patches that have been applied as recorded below). Sub-rows (M_i.1, M_i.2, ...) will be drafted before each prose block at finer granularity, as was done for H4.x, H6.x, H8.x, H9.x, and H10.x in Chapter 2. ChatGPT's recommended sub-row decomposition pattern is two blocks: Block A (MP1.x, MP2.x for §§1-2 first, drafted and audited together) and Block B (MP3.x-MP7.x for §§3-7, drafted and audited as a second block) to keep loops tight given Chapter 3's mathematical density.

The Chapter 3 bibliography prerequisites have been added to `dissertation_references.bib` for a total of 66 entries: `lynch1995simulations` (the canonical reference for the simulation/refinement family beyond bisimulation), `plotkin2004structural` (the canonical reference for structural operational semantics and labeled transition systems), `sangiorgi2012bisimulation` (the modern textbook reference for bisimulation theory), and `pierce2002types` (the standard reference for type-theoretic foundations). A pre-existing citation key mismatch was discovered and patched across three locations in the same cycle: Chapter 1 §2 pedigree paragraph, Chapter 2 §7.5, and Section 2 row A4 of this ledger all attributed to "Mac Lane and Moerdijk" but cited `maclane1998categories` (the sole-Mac-Lane *Categories for the Working Mathematician*); all three citation keys have been changed to `maclane1994sheaves` (the actual Mac Lane and Moerdijk *Sheaves in Geometry and Logic*) to match the prose attribution. The Section 2 A4 row patch was specifically surfaced by ChatGPT's spec-only audit on the Chapter 3 parent contract — an example of the audit cycle catching a structural-honesty gap that survived three Chapter 2 canon cycles undetected. The Chapter 2 §5.5 citation of `maclane1998categories` remains unchanged because that reference does not attribute to Moerdijk and is correctly pointing to the general categories book.

Five MP-row wording softenings were applied during this spec-only audit cycle to preserve the "Chapter 3 introduces machinery, Chapters 4-7 state the axioms" boundary: MP3 was softened to keep the relation-strength encoding flexible (optionally representable as a small category or preorder rather than committed to a small finite category at the parent-row level); MP4 was softened so that Chapter 3 introduces the versioned-surface apparatus and Chapter 4 will use it to state the append-only-provenance constraint, rather than Chapter 3 formalizing the constraint itself; MP5 was softened the same way (Chapter 3 introduces R_may and the caller-side coverage vocabulary, Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness requirement); MP6 was softened similarly (Chapter 3 introduces projection families, projection domains, partiality, and consistency-relation machinery, with the accounting-identity exemplars as motivation rather than as the axiom; Chapter 7 will state when defined projections are required to mutually cohere); and MP7 was softened so that Chapter 3 introduces the decidable-fragment discipline and identifies candidate decidable fragments, with rigorous decidability claims deferred to the relevant axiom chapters and Chapter 10.

The notation introduced once and used throughout the dissertation: substrate identifier $S$, public-surface family $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$, substrate-level entities $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$, observer model $O$, context set $K$, correspondence relation $R$, producer's declared outcome relation $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$, verifier's conservative over-approximation $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, projection family $\Pi_X$, and consistency relation $\sim_X$. Each symbol is introduced as a typed variable with explicit components; relationships among them are not yet asserted (relationships are the work of Chapters 4-7) | MP1 | proof-obligation |
| MP1.4 | §1.4 — Notation-versus-claim discipline. The §1.3 symbols are notation, not assertions: introducing $S$ does not assert anything about substrates; introducing $R$ does not assert that any specific correspondence relation holds; introducing $\Pi_X$ does not assert projection consistency. The notation supplies vocabulary for the axiom chapters; the axiom statements remain Chapters 4-7's work. This is the operational implementation at the Chapter-3 level of the "Chapter 3 introduces machinery, Chapters 4-7 state the axioms" boundary, which §1.4 forward-references | MP1 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 3 (notation-vs-axiom-statement boundary) | proof-obligation |

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MP2.1 | §2.1 — Public surfaces. Defined as the formal artifacts visible to callers, auditors, users, or other downstream verifiers: the published specification, the visible API, the disclosed audit attestation, a textual witness treated as authoritative within a transmission community. A public surface is a structured type with explicit components (declared interface, declared semantics, declared behavior expectations) but carries no constraints on what behavior the underlying substrate actually exhibits; that is the work of Axiom 2 in Chapter 5 | MP2 | proof-obligation |
| MP2.2 | §2.2 — Substrates. Defined as the underlying entities that surfaces describe, implement, summarize, or expose: the program whose API is the public surface, the organization whose financial position the financial-statement family projects, the manuscript tradition whose textual content the critical edition presents. A substrate is a structured type with explicit components (actual state, operational behavior, real interface) distinct from but related to the public surface's declarations | MP2 | proof-obligation |
| MP2.3 | §2.3 — Observer models. Defined as the formal limits on what a caller, verifier, auditor, or user can distinguish or detect when interacting with a substrate through its public surface. Different observer models correspond to different verification regimes: a refinement-type caller with the full type system available, an audit-style auditor with sampled access, a mass-transmission community of reciters with limited individual access but high aggregate coverage. The observer model parameterizes what a verifier can observe or distinguish in a given verification regime; the axiom chapters use that parameter when stating structural-honesty failures | MP2 | proof-obligation |
| MP2.4 | §2.4 — Contexts. Defined as the operational conditions under which surface-substrate consistency claims are evaluated: the workload range, the deployment environment, the audit scope, the textual-transmission community. Contexts parameterize what counts as "the substrate's relevant behavior" for the purposes of consistency evaluation. Later chapters may evaluate the same surface/substrate pair under different contexts $K_1$ and $K_2$, allowing context-sensitive consistency claims to be stated explicitly rather than left implicit | MP2 | proof-obligation |
| MP2.5 | §2.5 — Structured-type packaging and axiom deferral. Public surfaces, substrates, observer models, and contexts are packaged as structured types used by later chapters, with axiom-specific constraints explicitly deferred to Chapters 4-7. The packaging summary states: surfaces are objects with surface-type structure; substrates are objects with substrate-type structure; observer models are typed observation calculi; contexts are typed condition specifications. Subsequent axiom chapters will impose constraints that relate these objects (Axiom 1 on surface evolution; Axiom 2 on surface-substrate consistency under observer-model $O$; Axiom 3 on caller-side coverage of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; Axiom 4 on projection-family consistency) | MP2 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 (coverage-vs-formal-development drift) | proof-obligation |

**Block A coverage check.** The union of MP1.1-MP1.4 covers MP1 (notation foundations); the union of MP2.1-MP2.5 covers MP2 (domain objects). ### Chapter 3 §§3-7 sub-outline (Block B: correspondence-relation families, versioned surfaces, R_may, projection families, decidability)

These sub-rows refine MP3-MP7 into the specific subsection commitments that the §§3-7 prose will discharge. Same specification-first discipline as Block A and as the Chapter 2 sub-rows; finer granularity to control drift in the prose-writing phase. Sub-outline drafted by ChatGPT in collaboration with the dissertation's sole author, with verbose-claim expansion applied to match the existing H4.x and H6.x format conventions. The audit-risk anchoring in the discharges column follows ChatGPT's recommended pattern: MP3.6, MP4.3, MP5.2, and MP6.3 are tagged with Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 (coverage-vs-formal-development drift) where the prerequisite-vs-axiom boundary is most exposed; MP7.3 is tagged with audit-risk 4 (forward-reference discipline) where the candidate-versus-proven distinction is structurally important.

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MP3.1 | §3.1 — Correspondence-relation family as a structured collection. Defined as a parametric family of relations between public surfaces and substrate behaviors, from which a specific substrate-appropriate relation $R$ is selected per substrate. The family is not assumed to satisfy any consistency property at the §3.1 level; the family's structure (members, relationships among members, choice mechanism) is the focus of §3 prerequisites. Chapter 5 will use the relation family to state Axiom 2 by quantifying over the substrate's declared correspondence relation | MP3 | proof-obligation |
| MP3.2 | §3.2 — Labeled transition systems and structural operational semantics. The finite-state foundation for protocol-style correspondence relations: states, transitions, labels, and the structural operational semantics that generates transitions from program syntax [plotkin2004structural]. LTS provides the formal substrate over which bisimulation, simulation, and refinement relations are defined; SOS provides the syntactic generator. Chapter 3 introduces the LTS/SOS machinery; Chapter 5 will use it to define the relation-family members rigorously | MP3 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP3.3 | §3.3 — Bisimulation as the strongest standard finite-state behavioral equivalence. Defined as the symmetric correspondence relation in the Park-Milner sense [park1981concurrency, milner1980calculus, hennessy1985algebraic], with algorithmic foundations in Kanellakis-Smolka [kanellakis1990ccs] and modern theoretical treatment in Sangiorgi [sangiorgi2012bisimulation]. Bisimulation is treated as the strongest standard finite-state behavioral equivalence used in this dissertation, under the declared observer model and the usual finite/image-finite assumptions needed for the relevant modal-characterization results. Chapter 3 introduces the definition; Chapter 5 will state when bisimulation is the appropriate $R$ for a substrate | MP3 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP3.4 | §3.4 — Simulation and refinement as weaker correspondence relations. Defined where bisimulation is overstrong: simulation is the asymmetric directional version (one system can mimic another but not necessarily the converse); refinement is the related notion used in concurrency theory and distributed-systems verification [lynch1995simulations]. These relations are appropriate when the substrate-surface correspondence is asymmetric. Chapter 3 introduces the family members; Chapter 5 will state when each is the substrate-appropriate choice | MP3 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP3.5 | §3.5 — Abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality. Non-LTS correspondence forms appropriate for substrates where the public surface is a document, report, model card, or other non-transition-based artifact. Abstraction-preserving equivalence treats two structures as corresponding when they preserve a designated abstraction map between them; extraction equality treats two structures as corresponding when an extraction procedure (computed from one) produces an artifact matching the other. These forms generalize the LTS-based relations to substrates including philological texts, AI model cards, financial reports, and attestation documents. Chapter 3 introduces these correspondence forms; Chapter 5 will state when they are the substrate-appropriate choice | MP3 | proof-obligation |
| MP3.6 | §3.6 — Relation-choice mechanism. The relation-choice mechanism is the structured field by which a substrate records which correspondence relation $R$ from the family it will use. Chapter 5 will state the Axiom 2 requirement over that declared choice. The choice mechanism keeps the relation-family approach tractable: per-substrate declarations recorded as structured fields, rather than a single uniform relation across all substrates | MP3 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 (coverage-vs-formal-development drift) | proof-obligation |

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MP4.1 | §4.1 — Version-indexed public-surface families. Defined as a sequence $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ of public surfaces indexed by version, with each successive $S_{i+1}$ representing a published revision of $S_i$. The version index tracks the temporal evolution of the surface; the family is not assumed to satisfy any inheritance property at this point (that is stated as Axiom 1 in Chapter 4). Chapter 3 introduces the typed family; Chapter 4 will use it to state the append-only-provenance invariant | MP4 | proof-obligation |
| MP4.2 | §4.2 — Behavioral subtyping between versions. Defined as the Liskov-Wing inheritance relation [liskov1994behavioral] applied between $S_i$ and $S_{i+1}$ at the public-surface level: $S_{i+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ when callers programmed against $S_i$'s declared interface continue to function correctly against $S_{i+1}$'s declared interface. Chapter 3 introduces the behavioral-subtyping relation; Chapter 4 will use it when stating the Axiom 1 append-only-provenance discipline across the version-indexed surface family | MP4 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP4.3 | §4.3 — Compatible extension versus silent breaking change. The surface-level distinction between extension that preserves the behavioral-subtyping relation (additive evolution: new capabilities, new optional parameters, new endpoints that do not interfere with existing semantics) and silent breaking change (modification that violates the behavioral-subtyping relation without explicit corrigenda). Chapter 3 introduces the discrimination vocabulary; Chapter 4 will use this vocabulary to distinguish permitted compatible extensions from impermissible silent breaks | MP4 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 | proof-obligation |
| MP4.4 | §4.4 — Truth-status tags. Defined as explicit surface objects (correction, supersession, withdrawal) that mark changes to previously-declared content. A correction tag indicates that a prior claim was wrong and is revised; a supersession tag indicates that a prior claim is replaced by a newer claim that takes precedence; a withdrawal tag indicates that a prior claim is no longer maintained or defended. The tags are surface objects rather than silent mutations: the original declaration remains visible with the tag attached. Chapter 4 will use the tags to state the corrigenda discipline that distinguishes append-only-provenance with corrections from silent rewriting | MP4 | proof-obligation |
| MP4.5 | §4.5 — Historical-record preservation. The object-level apparatus that ensures the historical record across $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ remains accessible and verifiable. Each $S_i$ is preserved in archived form alongside its successors; corrections, supersessions, and withdrawals are recorded as additions rather than as deletions. Chapter 4 will use this apparatus to state the append-only-provenance invariant that Axiom 1 imposes; Chapter 3 supplies the typed objects (archived versions, corrigenda tags, retention discipline) | MP4 | proof-obligation |

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MP5.1 | §5.1 — $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as conservative over-approximation. Defined as the verifier's typed object representing the set of possible producer outcomes that a caller must be prepared to handle. The construction is conservative: $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ includes every outcome that the verifier cannot rule out, possibly more outcomes than the producer actually exhibits. The conservatism is what makes the construction tractable: the verifier need only over-approximate the actual outcome set, not compute it precisely. Chapter 3 introduces $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over it | MP5 | proof-obligation |
| MP5.2 | §5.2 — Distinguishing $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ from $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. The structural distinction between $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ (the producer's declared possible outcomes, introduced as a standing symbol in MP1.3 / Table 3.1) and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (the verifier's conservative over-approximation of possible outcomes). The verifier's approximation may include outcomes the producer does not declare; the caller must be prepared for the full $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ range. Chapter 3 introduces the distinction; Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness obligation over the relevant relationship between them | MP5 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 | proof-obligation |
| MP5.3 | §5.3 — Substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines. The methods by which $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is computed for different substrate types: type-level over-approximation in the refinement-type tradition [swamy2016fstar, vazou2014refinement] where the type system supplies the over-approximation; static-analysis over-approximation where a static analyzer enumerates possible outcomes with bounded depth [pierce2002types]; audit-style over-approximation where an auditor enumerates possible control-failure modes within a defined scope; document-extraction over-approximation where an automated extractor enumerates possible interpretations of an ambiguous document. Chapter 3 introduces the substrate-specific disciplines as parameterizations; Chapter 6 will state the axiom over the substrate's declared discipline | MP5 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP5.4 | §5.4 — Caller-side coverage vocabulary. Three discharge categories for caller-side handling of outcomes in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$: handled (the caller has explicit logic for the outcome), propagated-as-incomplete (the caller acknowledges the outcome and propagates it to its own caller with an incompleteness annotation), and proven-unreachable (the caller proves the outcome cannot occur in its context). Chapter 3 introduces the vocabulary; Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness axiom requiring every outcome in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ to fall into one of these three categories | MP5 | proof-obligation |
| MP5.5 | §5.5 — Caller obligations as extension of producer-side refinement types. The structural-honesty contribution to the refinement-type tradition: where the producer-side discipline (F\textsuperscript{$\star$}, Liquid Haskell) requires producers to satisfy refinements declared in their signatures, the dissertation's caller-side discipline additionally requires callers to discharge their obligations over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ in the three-category vocabulary of MP5.4. Chapter 3 positions the caller-side discipline as an extension of producer-side discipline; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 as the formal caller obligation | MP5 | cited + proof-obligation |

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MP6.1 | §6.1 — Projection family $\Pi_X$ as a finite structured family. Defined as a finite collection $\{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ of projections, each $\pi_i$ being a function from substrate-state to a typed view, indexed by substrate $X$. The family is finite by the finite-default convention (MP1.2); each member is a typed object with explicit domain and range. The family is not assumed to satisfy any consistency property at this point; consistency is the work of Chapter 7 | MP6 | proof-obligation |
| MP6.2 | §6.2 — Projection domains and partiality. Each projection $\pi_i$ has an explicit domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \subseteq \mathrm{Substrate}(X)$ over which it is defined; outside the domain, $\pi_i$ is partial. Different projections in the family may have different domains. The partiality is structurally important: a substrate fact need not be projectable into every member of $\Pi_X$, and later consistency checks can only be stated on regions where the relevant projections are jointly defined. Chapter 3 introduces the partiality structure; Chapter 7 will state when joint definability implies mutual coherence | MP6 | proof-obligation |
| MP6.3 | §6.3 — Substrate-specific consistency relations $\sim_X$. Defined as the substrate-specific relation later used to express when two projection outputs are compatible, where both are defined on the same underlying fact. The relation $\sim_X$ varies by substrate: arithmetic identity for double-entry bookkeeping, accounting identities for modern financial reporting, control-evidence-attestation consistency for security audit, variant-record-comparison for textual-preservation philology. Chapter 3 introduces the consistency-relation parameter without yet requiring mutual coherence; Chapter 7 will state when projections are required to cohere under $\sim_X$ | MP6 + Chapter-3 audit-risk 1 | proof-obligation |
| MP6.4 | §6.4 — Motivating projection-family examples. The dissertation's exemplar projection families serve as motivation for Axiom 4's structure: double-entry bookkeeping [pacioli1494] with $n = 2$ projections under arithmetic identity; modern financial reporting [previts1979history] with statement projections under jurisdiction-dependent accounting identities; multi-control audit [iso27001, nist80053, aicpa2017tsc] with scope/control/evidence/operation projections under attestation consistency; manuscript cross-witnessing [timpanaro2005lachmann, reynolds2013scribes, tov2012textual, strack1996introduction] with witness-line projections under stemmatic consistency; recitation chains [farrin2010surat, arfeen2026shv] with hifz/manuscript/tajwid/riwayat/communal-verification projections under multi-substrate cross-coherence; software-release projection families [arfeen2026shvsupplychain] with sigstore/in-toto/SLSA/SHV projections under supply-chain consistency. These are exemplars, not the axiom statement; Chapter 7 abstracts the pattern to substrate-parameterized form | MP6 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP6.5 | §6.5 — Sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary. The categorical language for compactly describing compatible projections: a projection family $\Pi_X$ over a substrate $X$ with consistency relation $\sim_X$ can be expressed as a sheaf-style condition over a small finite category, in the sense of Mac Lane and Moerdijk [maclane1994sheaves], where each projection corresponds to a section over an open set in the category, and consistency corresponds to compatibility under the sheaf's restriction maps. The categorical vocabulary supplies the formal apparatus for stating Axiom 4 compactly; Chapter 3 introduces the apparatus, Chapter 7 uses it to state the axiom | MP6 | cited + proof-obligation |
| MP6.6 | §6.6 — Deferral to Chapter 7. Chapter 7 will state when defined projections in $\Pi_X$ are required to mutually cohere under $\sim_X$ — that is, when the projection family is required to satisfy Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency). Chapter 3 supplies the typed projection family, the partiality structure, the substrate-specific consistency relation, the motivating exemplars, and the sheaf-style vocabulary; Chapter 7 supplies the axiom statement | MP6 | proof-obligation |

**Sub-outline audit risks (for the spec-only audit pass).** Five risks to check before sub-row decomposition or prose drafting begins:

1. **Coverage versus formal-development drift.** Chapter 3's role is to introduce the mathematical apparatus, not to develop Axioms 1-4 themselves. Each MP-row should introduce the machinery and stop short of stating or proving the axiom; the axiom development belongs to Chapters 4-7. The risk is that prose in MP3-MP6 starts to look like Chapter-4-7 prose if the axiom statement leaks into the prerequisites section.
2. **Bibliography sufficiency.** The 66-entry bibliography is now Chapter-2-complete and Chapter-3-prerequisite-complete, but Chapter 3 prose may surface additional needs (e.g., a specific decidability reference if MP7 develops the decidable-fragment discipline beyond informal statement, or a specific abstraction-refinement source if MP3 develops the correspondence-relation family beyond the four listed exemplars). The risk is silent bibliography gaps surfacing late in prose drafting.
3. **Notation-versus-axiom-statement boundary.** MP1 introduces standing notation; MP2-MP6 introduce domain-specific machinery. The risk is that MP1 prose starts to look like an axiom statement (e.g., a definition of "surface-substrate consistency" rather than a notation for it) or that MP2-MP6 use notation that MP1 did not introduce.
4. **Forward-reference discipline.** MP1-MP7 forward-reference Chapters 4-8 for axiom statements, Chapter 17 for open problems, and the four-substrate substrate work for the operational vocabulary. The risk is that forward references commit Chapter 3 to specific claims about future chapters that may not survive their own development. The discipline is to forward-reference in the form "Chapter k will develop X" rather than "Chapter k shows that X holds."
5. **Cross-section namespace consistency.** Every newly introduced row prefix or numbering scheme should be globally unique across the existing ledger. The risk is that a new prefix collides with an existing one (as the originally-drafted M1-M7 collided with Section 4's M1-M6, before the rename to MP1-MP7), producing ambiguous row identifiers. The discipline is to check the existing ledger for prefix and numbering conflicts before promoting any new ledger section to canon.

**Post-prose audit prompt (for §§1-7 once drafted).** "Audit Chapter 3 only against ledger rows MP1-MP7 and their sub-rows (to be drafted before each prose block). Identify (a) any claim not covered by MP1-MP7 or its sub-rows, (b) any place where the prose develops an axiom or theorem rather than introducing the machinery the axiom or theorem will use, (c) any notation in MP2-MP6 that MP1 did not introduce, (d) any forward reference that commits Chapter 3 to a specific claim about a later chapter's content, (e) any source that does not support the claim attached to it, (f) any place where the prose treats a decidability claim or limit as established when the chapter has not yet formally established it, and (g) any newly introduced row prefix or numbering scheme that is not globally unique across the existing ledger (the cross-section namespace consistency check). Do not review style except where wording creates a structural-honesty risk."

**Standing audit discipline (added May 12, 2026 following the MP1-MP7 namespace collision discovery; refined the same day to include spec-only audit coverage).** The cross-section namespace consistency check is now present in both audit prompts for Chapter 3: as risk 5 in the spec-only audit risks list (catching collisions before sub-rows or prose are drafted, where remediation is cheapest), and as clause (g) in the post-prose audit prompt (catching any collisions that survive the spec phase and surface in the prose stage). This addition was triggered by the spec-only audit cycle exposing a real collision between Section 4's M1-M6 (durability-mechanism operationalizations) and Section 11's originally-drafted M1-M7 (Chapter 3 mathematical prerequisites, now renamed to MP1-MP7). Neither auditor surfaced the collision because the audit prompts at the time did not ask for cross-section consistency checks. The clause now becomes a standing audit discipline for all subsequent sub-outline cycles in the dissertation: any new ledger row prefix or numbering scheme introduced for a new chapter or section should be checked against the existing ledger before promotion to canon. The recursive structural-honesty test on the ledger applies here as everywhere else: a row identifier that means two different things across the ledger is itself a structural-honesty gap, and the audit pattern needs an explicit detector for that gap pattern at both the spec-only and post-prose stages.

Total: 22 precision patches across the chapter, with each patch identified by either auditor (ChatGPT or Perplexity) and applied transparently.

## Section 12: Chapter 4 ledger rows (Axiom 1 — append-only provenance / versioned-surface honesty)

Chapter 4 is the first axiom chapter. Its structural role is to state and develop Axiom 1 (append-only provenance / versioned-surface honesty) over the version-indexed public-surface family, behavioral-subtyping apparatus, truth-status tags, and historical-record preservation introduced in Chapter 3 §4. Chapter 4 §1 contains the formal statement, conditions, failure modes, examples, and proof obligations; subsequent sections of Chapter 4 (if any) will be added to this section as additional parent rows or sub-rows when the §1 spec-only audit clarifies whether more chapter structure is needed.

The parent-row anchor for Chapter 4 is the existing A1 row at Section 2 (Chapter 1 §2: four-axiom synthesis), which carries the proof obligation that Chapter 4 will discharge. The sub-rows A1.1-A1.7 below decompose that proof obligation into seven per-subsection commitments. The decomposition follows the user-author's recommended structure (May 12, 2026) and is verbose-expanded to match the H4.x and MP_k.j format conventions established for Chapters 2 and 3.

### Chapter 4 §1 sub-outline (Axiom 1 statement and development, specification-first, pre-prose)

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1.1 | §1.1 — Formal statement of Axiom 1 over version-indexed public-surface family. Chapter 4 §1.3 formalizes the corrigenda-discipline requirement: every breaking version transition has a corresponding tag specifying which prior surface element is modified, what kind of modification, and when it takes effect | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.4 prerequisites (MP4.4) | proof-obligation |

Chapter 4 §1.4 formalizes the historical-record preservation condition as part of Axiom 1 | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.5 prerequisites (MP4.5) | proof-obligation |

Chapter 4 §1.5 explains how each corresponds to a violation of one or more A1.1-A1.4 conditions, with exhaustiveness deferred to Chapter 8 | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.3 (silent breaking change as pattern, per MP4.3) | proof-obligation |

### Chapter 4 §§2-3 sub-outline (Axiom 1 edge cases and Chapter 5 handoff, specification-first, pre-prose)

The architectural decision (May 12, 2026) following Chapter 4 §1 canon: extend Chapter 4 beyond §1 to include two additional sections covering Axiom 1's behavior in difficult cases and the bridge to Chapter 5. | A1.8 | §2.1 — Corrigendum-on-corrigendum. When a truth-status tag itself turns out to be wrong (a correction was misapplied, a supersession was incorrectly invoked, a withdrawal was made hastily), Axiom 1 permits a meta-corrigendum: a corrigendum tag with explicit reference to the prior tag it modifies. The structural requirement is recursive: the meta-corrigendum is itself a truth-status tag, and Axiom 1 applies to it as it applies to any surface element. Chapter 4 §2.1 formalizes the recursive corrigendum structure | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.4 (truth-status tags as surface objects) | proof-obligation |
| A1.9 | §2.2 — Mistaken withdrawal. A specific instance of the corrigendum-on-corrigendum pattern: when a withdrawal tag was applied to a claim that should have been retained or corrected rather than withdrawn. The mistaken-withdrawal pattern is structurally reversible via a meta-correction-or-supersession tag that restores or supersedes the withdrawn claim. Chapter 4 §2.2 details the mistaken-withdrawal scenario | A1 + A1.8 (recursive corrigendum structure) | proof-obligation |
| A1.10 | §2.3 — Supersession chains. When a claim is superseded multiple times in sequence ($S_i$'s claim → $S_{i+1}$'s replacement → $S_{i+2}$'s further replacement), each supersession transition carries its own supersession tag, and the supersession chain is navigable through the corrigenda register. The chain does not collapse: each intermediate claim remains visible in the historical record per §1.4's archived-versions condition. Chapter 4 §2.3 formalizes the supersession-chain structure | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.4 + Chapter 3 §4.5 | proof-obligation |
| A1.11 | §2.4 — Deprecation timelines. Withdrawal tags often carry a deprecation timeline structure: a claim is announced as deprecated (intent-to-withdraw signal), then deprecated (active deprecation period), then removed (formal withdrawal). The timeline structure is part of the withdrawal tag and is recorded in the corrigenda register alongside the tag. Chapter 4 §2.4 formalizes the deprecation-timeline structure for withdrawal tags | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.4 | proof-obligation |
| A1.12 | §2.5 — Archive loss as historical-record preservation failure. §2.5 treats archive loss as the canonical edge case for the historical-record preservation condition of §1.4. Archive loss occurs when predecessor surfaces, corrigenda registers, or retained archives are no longer accessible for the period during which the surface's claims may be relied upon. This is not introduced as a fourth exhaustive peer category alongside the §1.5 primary patterns; it is a preservation-side failure of Axiom 1 whose relationship to the §1.5 taxonomy is deferred to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy analysis | A1 + Chapter 3 §4.5 (historical-record preservation) + §1.4 preservation condition | proof-obligation |
| A1.13 | §2.6 — Version-history forks. ### Chapter 5 §1 sub-outline (Axiom 2 statement and development, specification-first, pre-prose)

**Pre-decomposition architectural verification (May 12, 2026).** Before drafting the A2.X sub-row decomposition, the prerequisite machinery for Axiom 2 was verified in Chapter 3. Chapter 3 §2 establishes the four domain objects as a structured type system: public surfaces (§2.1), substrates (§2.2), observer models O (§2.3), and contexts K (§2.4), with §2.5 packaging and the explicit axiom-deferral note stating "Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) will constrain surface-substrate consistency under observer model O and context K for a chosen correspondence relation R". Chapter 3 §3 establishes the correspondence-relation family with the relation-choice mechanism (§3.6). The A2 parent row at Section 2 commits to "Surface-substrate consistency under declared observer model and context set, with R drawn from family of correspondence relations". All machinery Axiom 2 quantifies over is already canonical in Chapter 3, and the A2 parent row's scope is consistent with the proposed sub-row decomposition. No Chapter 3 patches are needed and no new typed objects are introduced in Chapter 5; Chapter 5 quantifies over already-stable Chapter 3 machinery exactly as Chapter 4 quantified over the Chapter 3 §4 versioned-surface machinery. The pre-decomposition verification step is now elevated to standing discipline: before drafting any axiom-chapter sub-row decomposition, verify that the prerequisite typed objects are in canon and that the parent-row commitment is consistent with the proposed decomposition. The verification step would have caught a hypothetical "introduce O and K natively in Chapter 5" architectural detour that this cycle nearly pursued before checking what was already in Chapter 3.

| ID | Claim | Discharges | Status |
|---|---|---|---|

Axiom 2 states that for every substrate $S$ with public surface $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ and substrate object $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$, declared observer model $O$ (Chapter 3 §2.3), declared context set $K$ (Chapter 3 §2.4), and declared correspondence relation $R$ (Chapter 3 §3, chosen from the family), the consistency condition $R(\mathrm{Surface}(S), \mathrm{Substrate}(S))$ holds at the observability level $O$ permits within the operational conditions specified by $K$. The axiom is a claim of surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$, not a claim of full truth | A2 + Chapter 3 §2.1-§2.4 (domain objects) + Chapter 3 §3 (correspondence-relation family) | proof-obligation |

| A2.3 | §1.3 — Context-set declaration discipline. **Sub-outline audit risks (for the Chapter 5 spec-only audit pass).** Ten risks to check before sub-row decomposition is finalized or prose drafting begins:

1. **Axiom-statement-vs-axiom-proof drift.** Chapter 5's role is to state Axiom 2 and develop its conditions, not to prove Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy theorem or Chapter 10's decidability/quantum-survivability theorems. The risk is that A2.5 (satisfaction condition) or A2.8 (proof obligations) drifts into Chapter 8 content.
2. **Prerequisite-reuse precision.** A2.1-A2.15 quantify over Chapter 3 §2 typed objects (surfaces, substrates, O, K), Chapter 3 §3 R-family with relation-choice mechanism, Chapter 3 §5 $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ for the Chapter 6 handoff, and Chapter 3 §7 finite-default fragment. The risk is loose vocabulary usage of objects the prerequisite chapter defined precisely.
3. **Consistency-not-truth discipline (A2-specific).** Axiom 2 is consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$, not a claim of full truth or universal correspondence. The risk is that the prose collapses consistency-under-declaration into truth-simpliciter, especially in A2.5 (satisfaction condition) and A2.7 (substrate examples).
4. **Failure-mode-exhaustiveness drift.** A2.6 identifies three primary failure patterns. The risk is that this is read as claiming the three-pattern set is exhaustive; the mitigation in A2.6 explicitly defers exhaustiveness to Chapter 8.
5. **Four-substrate example fidelity.** A2.7 illustrates Axiom 2 across SI1-SI4 with substrate-appropriate $(O, K, R)$ for each. The risk is that the substrate-specific $(O, K, R)$ claims depend on substrate-specific properties not yet established in Chapter 5.
6. **Chapter 8 overcommit.** A2.8 forward-references Chapter 8. The risk is "Chapter 8 will show" or "Chapter 8 establishes" rather than "Chapter 8 is assigned" or "Chapter 8 will evaluate".
7. **Chapter 6 overcommit.** A2.14 and A2.15 forward-reference Chapter 6. The risk is pre-stating Axiom 3's R_may caller-coverage content rather than only naming the structural dependency.
8. **Joint-axiom interaction risk.** A2.10 (K-change routing through Axiom 1), A2.11 (R-change routing through Axiom 1), and A2.12 (joint Axiom-1-Axiom-2 interaction more broadly) all address how Axioms 1 and 2 interact. The risk is that the prose re-states either axiom rather than only naming the structural interaction: Axiom 1 governs public-surface evolution (including evolution of K and R when they are on the public surface); Axiom 2 supplies the consistency claim at whatever surface version, K, and R are current.
9. **Cross-section namespace consistency.** A2.1-A2.15 extend the A2.X sub-row numbering. The risk is that the .1-.15 numbering collides with any sub-row scheme in subsequent chapters that use the same parent row.
10. **Within-section internal-consistency.** Every audit-risk text and audit-prompt clause must reflect the sub-row content. The risk (now elevated to standing discipline from the Chapter 4 §1 Risk-4/A1.6 and Chapter 4 §§2-3 Risk-5/A1.15 occurrences) is that any patch to a sub-row leaves a stale reference in the audit-risk list or audit-prompt clause.

**Spec-only audit prompt for Chapter 5 sub-outline.** "Audit Chapter 5 §§1-3 sub-outline only against parent row A2 (at Section 2) and sub-rows A2.1-A2.15. Identify any sub-row that develops an axiom other than Axiom 2 or pre-states Chapter 6's Axiom 3 content; any sub-row that misuses Chapter 3 §2, §3, §5, or §7 prerequisite vocabulary; any sub-row that collapses surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$ into a full-truth claim; any sub-row that claims A2.6's three-pattern set is exhaustive without forward-reference to Chapter 8; any A2.7 substrate-specific $(O, K, R)$ assignment that depends on substrate-specific properties not yet established; any Chapter 8 forward-reference that overcommits (e.g., 'will show' rather than 'will evaluate'); any A2.12 prose that re-states Axioms 1 or 2 rather than naming the structural interaction; any source that does not support the attached claim; any row prefix or numbering scheme that collides with existing ledger identifiers; and any audit-risk text or audit-prompt clause that quotes pre-patch sub-row wording after the sub-row has been patched."

| A3.2 | §1.2 — $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ versus $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ in the caller-side obligation. Following Chapter 3 §5.2, Axiom 3 quantifies over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ — the verifier's conservative over-approximation — not over $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ (the producer's tighter Axiom 2 claim). The structural reason: even when the producer's $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ correctly identifies a narrow set of actual producer outcomes, the caller cannot in general verify that the producer's $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ is exhaustive, so the caller must reason about the conservative over-approximation $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. The $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ overhead is the structural-honesty cost of caller-side reasoning under conservative producer-side claim-verification | A3 + Chapter 3 §5.2 (R_declared vs R_may distinction) | proof-obligation |
| A3.3 | §1.3 — Caller-side observation regime. A3.3 formalizes the Chapter 5 §3.2 handoff vocabulary: a caller-side observation regime records the caller's observed features, contexts, and correspondence assumptions for purposes of evaluating its obligations over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. The caller has a typed observation calculus (its own observer model, analogous to but distinct from the producer's declared $O$), declared contexts (analogous to but distinct from the producer's declared $K$), and correspondence assumptions about producer outcomes (analogous to but distinct from the producer's declared $R$). The caller's coverage scope is the set of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified producer outcomes the caller must address; the scope is determined by the intersection of the producer's $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ with the caller's observation regime. The formalization here is the explicit Chapter 6 inheritance of the Chapter 5 §3.2 vocabulary that was scoped at that time as Chapter-6-facing | A3 + Chapter 3 §2.3-§2.4 (observer models, contexts) + Chapter 5 §3.2 (caller-observation-regime handoff, now formalized here) | proof-obligation |
| A3.4 | §1.4 — Three discharge paths from Chapter 3 §5.4. For every $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified producer outcome within the caller's coverage scope, the caller follows one of the three canonical discharge paths established in Chapter 3 §5.4: \emph{handled} (the caller provides an explicit case for the outcome — code path, audit response, model behavior, attestation handling, or substrate-appropriate handling); \emph{propagated-as-incomplete} (the caller declares the outcome as not-yet-handled and propagates the obligation to the caller's own callers, with the propagation recorded on the caller's surface as a structural-honesty declaration); \emph{proven-unreachable} (the caller proves the outcome cannot occur in the caller's operational context, with the supporting invariant recorded on the caller's surface). The three paths together exhaust the obligations a caller has for $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified outcomes; Axiom 3 requires that the caller's surface declare which path applies to each outcome | A3 + Chapter 3 §5.4 (three discharge categories) + Chapter 3 §5.5 (caller-obligation extension of refinement-type discipline) + cited: swamy2016fstar, vazou2014refinement | cited + proof-obligation |
| A3.5 | §1.5 — Three primary failure patterns. Within the Chapter 6 formalization, Axiom 3 has three primary failure patterns: \emph{unaddressed outcome} (an $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified producer outcome within the caller's coverage scope is not handled, not propagated-as-incomplete, and not proven-unreachable — the caller's surface is silent about the outcome); \emph{hidden propagation} (an outcome is implicitly propagated via runtime fault, exception bubble, silent failure, or comparable substrate-specific mechanism, without the caller's surface declaring the propagation, so the caller's own callers cannot determine the discharge path); \emph{false unreachability claim} (the caller claims proven-unreachable, but the supporting invariant does not actually hold under the caller's operational context). Exhaustiveness deferred to Chapter 8 | A3 + A3.4 + Chapter 8 forward reference | proof-obligation |
| A3.6 | §1.6 — Examples across SI1-SI4. For each worked substrate instance, the caller-side exhaustiveness obligation operationalizes through illustrative candidate discharge of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified outcomes. SI1 Bayyinah: callers (downstream tools consuming scanner outputs) discharge declared file kinds (handle each with a case), scan-incomplete primitive (propagate-as-incomplete), and out-of-scope file types (proven-unreachable via scope restriction). SI2 Furqan: callers (programs being type-checked, downstream compilers) discharge typed-program cases (handle), type-check failures (propagate-as-incomplete to diagnostic surface), and unused type-system features (proven-unreachable via program-context restriction). SI3 Munafiq: callers (eval pipelines, downstream judges) discharge declared markers (handle), marker-uncertainty (propagate-as-incomplete), and prompt-types excluded by caller context (proven-unreachable). SI4 Supply-chain: callers (consumers of attestations across the four layers) discharge attestation cases (handle), attestation-uncertainty (propagate-as-incomplete), and substrate states the caller's context excludes (proven-unreachable). The examples are illustrative candidate discharge assignments; substantive adequacy of these candidates is deferred to Chapter 8 and Chapters 13-16 | A3 + four-substrate scope (SI1-SI4 at Section 5) + Chapter 8 + Chapters 13-16 forward references | cited + proof-obligation |
| A3.7 | §1.7 — Proof obligations and Chapter 8 forward reference. Three proof obligations within Chapter 6: \emph{well-formedness} (Axiom 3 is well-formed over Chapter 3 §5 $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ machinery and the caller-side observation regime); \emph{decidability scope} (Axiom 3's exhaustiveness check is a candidate for decidable treatment in the finite-default fragment of Chapter 3 §7, assuming finite $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcomes, finite caller-side discharge specifications, and decidable invariant-verification for proven-unreachable claims, with Chapter 10 carrying the rigorous decidability burden and Chapter 8 §2's finite-witness construction (T82) operating within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes); \emph{exhaustiveness of the three failure patterns of A3.5} (Chapter 8 definitional-adequacy obligation). 8. **Chapter 7 overcommit.** A3.13 and A3.14 forward-reference Chapter 7. The A3.13/A3.14 reframing captures an important architectural insight: the four axioms do not form a strict linear dependency chain (A1 → A2 → A3 → A4) but a more flexible structure where each axiom can be stated independently and the satisfaction or failure of earlier axioms supplies inputs to later analyses. Axiom 1 governs surface evolution and is presupposed by every other axiom (because every axiom quantifies over public surfaces that evolve). Axiom 2 evaluates per-version consistency; its satisfaction supplies inputs to Axiom 3's caller-coverage analysis but is not a syntactic precondition for stating Axiom 3 (per the Chapter 5 §3.2/§3.3 patches). Axiom 3 evaluates caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; its caller-side artifacts may participate in Axiom 4's projection-consistency analysis as members of or inputs to projection families, but Axiom 4 is statable over $\Pi_X$ independently. The structural-honesty discipline of the four axioms allows each to be invoked independently while supplying useful inputs when satisfied. This is now the architectural pattern documented across Chapters 4, 5, and 6.

The §1.2 patch is methodologically instructive. The pre-patch phrasing was acceptable but treated the verifier's conservativeness as if it operated in a context-free sense. The patched phrasing correctly grounds the conservativeness in Chapter 3 §5.3's declared over-approximation discipline (the substrate-specific methods by which $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is computed for different substrate types: type-level over-approximation in F\textsuperscript{*} and Liquid Haskell, static-analysis enumeration, audit-style enumeration, document-extraction enumeration). The patched phrasing therefore reads as "conservative relative to the declared discipline" rather than "absolutely conservative" — a structurally important precision that prevents over-claiming the conservativeness of any particular $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ construction.

The §1.6 SI2 patch is the more substantive of the two required patches. Programs being type-checked are inputs to the type-checker, not callers of it — they are the substrate that the type-checker operates over. The actual callers are downstream consumers of the type-checker's output: compilers that build on the type-check results, CI pipelines that gate on the type-check outcome, developer tools that surface type-check diagnostics, and program authors who receive the diagnostics through their development environment. The category error — treating the program being type-checked as a caller — would have propagated a structurally inaccurate framing of the caller-side discipline through Chapter 6. ChatGPT's catch preserves the caller-side framing's accuracy.

The §1.3 clarification adds explicit hardening against a possible misreading where a reader might interpret the caller-side observation regime as a second producer-side $(O, K, R)$ declaration. The patched paragraph explicitly states these components are caller-side parameters used to determine which $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-identified outcomes fall within the caller's coverage scope — not producer-side declarations of substrate consistency. This protects the asymmetry between producer-side (Axiom 2 territory) and caller-side (Axiom 3 territory) that the dissertation depends on.

The §§2-3 post-prose patches are methodologically instructive. The §2.2 patch catches a subtle over-claim: "outcomes the prior $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ included but the new $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ excludes can be reclassified by callers as proven-unreachable" elides the requirement that proven-unreachable claims need supporting invariants. Mere exclusion from the new $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ removes the outcome from the caller's coverage scope (no Axiom-3 obligation), but doesn't automatically license a proven-unreachable classification (which would require the caller to record an invariant explaining why the outcome cannot occur in the caller's operational context). The patched phrasing preserves the structural-honesty distinction between scope-removal and invariant-based unreachability.

The §2.4 and §3.3 patches together catch a subtle pattern of over-claiming the independent-statability discipline. The pre-patch §2.4 said "Axiom 1 is presupposed because every other axiom quantifies over evolving public surfaces" — but the other axioms quantify over per-version surfaces and can be stated against a single version even when Axiom 1 has not been evaluated. The pre-patch §3.3 said "statable independently of the others" — but the axioms share Chapter 3 machinery (the typed objects, the correspondence-relation family, the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ machinery, the projection families) and consume each other's analytical artifacts. The patched phrasings preserve the correct claim — each axiom can be stated without requiring satisfaction of the others, with structural interaction operating through input-supply rather than precondition-stacking — without overclaiming either presupposition or total isolation.

| A4.1 | §1.1 — Formal statement of Axiom 4. For every substrate $X$ and every projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ declared over $X$ (Chapter 3 §6.1) with substrate-specific consistency relation $\sim_X$ (Chapter 3 §6.3), Axiom 4 requires that for every pair of projections $(\pi_i, \pi_j)$ in $\Pi_X$ and every substrate fact $s \in \mathrm{Substrate}(X)$ jointly defined under both projections ($s \in \mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_j)$ per Chapter 3 §6.2), the projection outputs satisfy $\pi_i(s) \sim_X \pi_j(s)$. This is Axiom 4: substrate-parameterized projection consistency over $\Pi_X$ under $\sim_X$. Axiom 4 is about consistency among declared projections within the family under the declared substrate-specific consistency relation, not about absolute truth of the substrate, not about total reconstruction of the substrate from the projections, and not about dependence on Axiom 3 satisfaction | A4 + Chapter 3 §6 (MP6.1, MP6.2, MP6.3 — full $\Pi_X$ machinery) | proof-obligation |
| A4.2 | §1.2 — Projection family $\Pi_X$ and projection-domain partiality. Following Chapter 3 §6.1 (MP6.1), the projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ is a finite structured family of projections from substrate states to typed views, indexed by the substrate $X$. Each $\pi_i$ has explicit domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \subseteq \mathrm{Substrate}(X)$ over which it is defined (Chapter 3 §6.2, MP6.2); outside its domain, $\pi_i$ is partial. Different projections in the family may have different domains. The partiality structure is what makes Axiom 4 statable: the consistency condition operates only on substrate states where the relevant projections are jointly defined, not on substrate states where one or more projections is undefined. This avoids spurious "inconsistency" claims when projections simply do not apply | A4 + Chapter 3 §6.1 (MP6.1) + Chapter 3 §6.2 (MP6.2) | proof-obligation |
| A4.3 | §1.3 — Substrate-specific consistency relation $\sim_X$. Following Chapter 3 §6.3 (MP6.3), the substrate-specific consistency relation $\sim_X$ is the relation expressing when two projection outputs are compatible. The relation varies by substrate: arithmetic identity for double-entry bookkeeping [pacioli1494], accounting identities for modern financial reporting [previts1979history], control-evidence-attestation consistency for security audit [iso27001, nist80053, aicpa2017tsc], variant-record comparison for textual-preservation philology [timpanaro2005lachmann, reynolds2013scribes, tov2012textual], multi-substrate cross-coherence for recitation chains [farrin2010surat, arfeen2026shv], supply-chain attestation consistency for software-release stacks [arfeen2026shvsupplychain]. Axiom 4 is parameterized by $\sim_X$ as part of the substrate's declared structure, not by a universal consistency relation; the axiom evaluates consistency relative to the declared $\sim_X$, parallel to the Axiom 2 relativization to declared $(O, K, R)$ | A4 + Chapter 3 §6.3 (MP6.3) + Chapter 3 §6.4 (MP6.4 motivating examples) | cited + proof-obligation |
| A4.4 | §1.4 — Joint-domain discipline. Axiom 4's consistency condition operates over joint-domain regions of the projection family. For two projections $\pi_i$ and $\pi_j$ in $\Pi_X$, the joint-domain region is $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_j)$; the consistency check $\pi_i(s) \sim_X \pi_j(s)$ is evaluated at substrate states $s$ in this region. For more than two projections, the joint domain is the multi-way intersection. Outside the joint-domain region, projections do not need to cohere because at least one is undefined. The joint-domain discipline distinguishes Axiom 4 from a stronger condition (total reconstructibility of the substrate from the projection family — Axiom 4 does not require this) and from a weaker condition (pairwise consistency only at hand-picked points — Axiom 4 requires consistency at every substrate state in every relevant joint-domain region). The elementary pairwise joint-domain formulation of A4.1 is the primary Chapter 7 statement of Axiom 4; the sheaf-style / commuting-diagram vocabulary from Chapter 3 §6.5 (MP6.5) [maclane1994sheaves] supplies a compact notational rendering when restriction maps and local-view overlaps are explicitly modeled, but Chapter 7 does not require the full topos-theoretic sheaf apparatus as part of the axiom statement | A4 + Chapter 3 §6.2 (MP6.2 partiality) + Chapter 3 §6.5 (MP6.5 sheaf-style vocabulary, as compact rendering) | cited + proof-obligation |
| A4.5 | §1.5 — Three primary failure patterns. Within the Chapter 7 formalization, Axiom 4 has three primary failure patterns. \emph{Projection inconsistency}: two or more projections are jointly defined at $s$, but their outputs do not satisfy $\sim_X$ — the canonical Axiom 4 violation, where projections that should cohere at $s$ do not. \emph{Hidden joint-domain use}: the public surface or verifier practice relies on projections as mutually comparable over a region not declared as part of the relevant joint domain — the structural-honesty failure is the gap between declared joint-domain scope and operational use scope (a domain-scope honesty failure, not a projection-output mismatch). \emph{False joint-domain declaration}: the surface declares that a projection or joint-domain restriction applies, but the declared domain condition does not actually hold for the substrate state being projected — the structural-honesty failure is the false domain declaration. These are primary A4 failure patterns, induced by projections, joint domains, and $\sim_X$; exhaustiveness across SI1-SI4 is deferred to Chapter 8 | A4 + A4.4 + Chapter 8 forward reference | proof-obligation |

**Sub-outline audit risks (for the Chapter 7 spec-only audit pass).** Thirteen risks to check before sub-row decomposition is finalized or prose drafting begins:

1. **Axiom-statement-vs-axiom-proof drift.** Chapter 7's role is to state Axiom 4 and develop its conditions, closing the statement-level development of AX-SH, not to prove Chapter 8's mutual-independence (T81), consistency (T82), or definitional-adequacy (T83) theorems.
2. **Prerequisite-reuse precision.** A4.1-A4.14 quantify over Chapter 3 §6 $\Pi_X$, partiality, and $\sim_X$ machinery (MP6.1-MP6.6), the Chapter 3 §7 finite-default fragment, and Chapters 4-5-6 axiom machinery. The risk is loose vocabulary usage.
3. **Projection-consistency-not-truth discipline (A4-specific).** Axiom 4 is about consistency among declared projections under declared $\sim_X$; it is not a claim of absolute substrate truth, not a claim of total reconstructibility, and not a claim of dependence on Axiom 3 satisfaction. The risk is conflating projection consistency with substrate truth.
4. **Joint-domain-not-everywhere discipline (A4-specific).** Axiom 4's consistency condition operates over joint-domain regions, not over all substrate states. The risk is treating the consistency condition as universal (which would require total reconstructibility) or as restricted to hand-picked points (which would be too weak).
5. **Failure-mode-exhaustiveness drift.** A4.5 identifies three primary failure patterns. The risk is claiming the three-pattern set is exhaustive; the mitigation in A4.5 explicitly defers exhaustiveness to Chapter 8.
6. **Four-substrate example fidelity.** A4.6 illustrates Axiom 4 across SI1-SI4 with candidate $\Pi_X$ and $\sim_X$. The risk is substrate-specific projection-family or consistency-relation claims that depend on substrate-specific properties not yet established.
7. **Chapter 8 overcommit.** A4.7, A4.13, and A4.14 forward-reference Chapter 8. The risk is "will show" or "establishes" rather than "is assigned" or "will evaluate", and particularly the risk of overcommitting T81 (mutual independence), T82 (consistency), or T83 (definitional adequacy) as already-proven rather than as Chapter 8 obligations.
8. **Closer-of-four-axiom-development framing.** Chapter 7 closes the four-axiom statement development; Chapter 8 is the integrative chapter. The risk is treating Chapter 7's §3.2-§3.3 as a continuation rather than as a closer, or conversely treating Chapter 7 as proving the four-axiom system rather than as completing its statement.
9. **Joint-axiom interaction risk.** A4.11 addresses A1-A2-A3-A4 interaction. The risk is re-stating any of the four axioms rather than naming the structural interaction; the further risk is overclaiming what the four axioms together prove (which is Chapter 8's job).
10. **Adversarial-declaration / under-determination risk.** Axioms 2, 3, and 4 are relativized to declared objects ($O$, $K$, $R$, $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, $\Pi_X$, $\sim_X$), creating a possible trivial-satisfaction route through adversarially weak declarations. Chapter 7 must not claim this concern is resolved. The cross-axiom checking pattern (A1 catches scope-narrowing through corrigenda; A3 catches under-declaration through caller-side failure; A4 catches projection-restriction through joint-domain failure) is the dissertation's candidate mitigation, but its sufficiency is a Chapter 8 obligation: Chapter 8 must evaluate whether cross-axiom interaction, operational vocabulary, and falsifiability witnesses prevent trivial satisfaction within the scoped substrate instances. T81 (mutual independence), T82 (consistency), and T83 (definitional adequacy) are the Chapter 8 theorems that address this collectively. Chapter 7 sub-rows should preserve the concern as a Chapter 8 obligation rather than imply the cross-axiom pattern already solves it.
11. **Cross-section namespace consistency.** A4.1-A4.14 extend the A4.X sub-row numbering. The risk is .1-.14 numbering colliding with any sub-row scheme in subsequent chapters using the same parent row.
12. **Within-section internal-consistency.** Every audit-risk text and audit-prompt clause must reflect the sub-row content. The risk (now elevated to standing discipline after three occurrences) is that any patch to a sub-row leaves a stale reference.
13. **Pre-decomposition architectural verification.** The fourth standing meta-check confirms prerequisite typed objects are in canon and parent-row commitment is consistent with the proposed decomposition. The verification has run for Chapter 7 (above) and all prerequisites are canonical — including the unusually rich Chapter 3 §6 MP6.1-MP6.6 machinery; the risk is that subsequent edits introduce non-canonical machinery.
